three-year-old son.  in the face of severe food shortages and inflated prices, a mother in her twenties resorted to purchasing a 400-gram can of materna plus 2 formula for her infant, rakan, from a small vendor within the camp in early august. the cost was 100 shekels, a significant increase from the pre-war price of 25 to 30 shekels. driven by her child's distress, she stated, "i wasn't thinking about the price. i was just looking for something to quiet rakan's crying. he was screaming from hunger. all i wanted was for him to calm down, to feel full for even a moment, even if it was just for a short time." it was only after the purchase, as rawan was about to open the can, that she observed the expiration date of february 2025. nevertheless, she felt she had no other alternatives. driven by her child's evident hunger, she resolved to proceed. with tears streaming down her face, she recounted her dilemma: "i considered returning the product, but they wouldn’t refund me, and finding another can seemed impossible, so i made the choice to take it and feed him." tragically, within a day of consuming the expired milk, rakan experienced adverse effects: "he developed severe diarrhea and intense stomach cramps, and cried incessantly." rawan carried him from one place to another, desperately seeking medicine or basic care, but pharmacies were rarely open, and hospitals lacked the resources to adequately address the situation. "the doctors cautioned me that my son might vomit or suffer from cramps, and, in the worst-case scenario, it could escalate to food poisoning. but i had no other options. even if i resolved to stop giving it to him, what could i offer? water? clean water is also unavailable." she added sorrowfully, glancing at her weary child's face, "i know giving him that milk is wrong." "it's a heartbreaking end, but if you could see the hunger in his eyes, you would understand. i had to choose the lesser of two evils."  al-turkmani: we haven't received any complaints or reports about the sale of expired medications. bakr al-turkmani, a lawyer and investigations coordinator at the independent commission for human rights (ichr), the ombudsman's office in the gaza strip, has indicated that the commission has not received any formal grievances or incident reports pertaining to the distribution of expired or counterfeit pharmaceutical products since the onset of hostilities. mr. al-turkmani further noted the absence of precise estimations or dependable data to accurately assess the prevalence of this issue, both within established pharmacies and in unregulated markets. he attributed this situation to the extensive disruption of gaza's administrative and institutional framework, resulting from direct israeli targeting, which has impacted all state institutions, including those responsible for accountability and regulatory oversight. mr. al-turkmani emphasized that the occupation’s military actions have specifically targeted members of the legislative council, civilian police personnel, and officials within various ministries and governmental agencies—the very entities tasked with monitoring, price regulation, and legal prosecution of offenders. al-turkmani asserted that the systematic nature of these attacks has eroded the accountability framework, fostering an environment of lawlessness. he posited that the objective is to destabilize the gaza strip by inciting disorder and disrupting civil peace and public order. he further noted that the targeting has extended beyond official institutions to encompass local and international aid workers and human rights advocates, including...
